gloss: The freedom to govern yourself or make your own decisions.
examples: The region was granted a degree of *autonomy* after the treaty.
Teachers at this school have a lot of *autonomy* in the classroom.
She values her *autonomy* more than a bigger salary.

gloss: A device that steers an aircraft or ship without a person controlling it.
examples: The captain switched on the *autopilot* once we reached cruising altitude.
I drove home on *autopilot* and barely remember the trip.
Big jets carry two independent *autopilots*.

gloss: Extreme greed for money or possessions.
examples: The novel is a study of *avarice* and what it costs.
Critics blamed the collapse on plain *avarice*.
His *avarice* eventually drove away every friend he had.

gloss: Someone who punishes a person for a wrong done to themselves or others.
examples: In the legend, the son becomes his father's *avenger*.
The movie's hero is less a detective than an *avenger*.
*Avengers* in these stories rarely find the peace they wanted.

gloss: A strong dislike of something.
examples: She has a strong *aversion* to loud parties.
He developed an *aversion* to shellfish after getting sick.
My *aversion* to needles started in childhood.

gloss: A person who flies an aircraft, especially in the early days of flying.
examples: Early *aviators* flew without radios or radar.
The museum honors a pioneering *aviator* from this state.
He wore the round sunglasses that *aviators* made famous.

gloss: The act of keeping away from something or preventing it from happening.
examples: Tax *avoidance* is legal; tax evasion is not.
*Avoidance* only makes the anxiety worse over time.
His *avoidance* of the subject told us everything.

gloss: A moment when someone suddenly understands or begins to feel something.
examples: His first paycheck was a rude *awakening*.
The book describes her political *awakening*.
Both brothers had similar spiritual *awakenings* in their thirties.

gloss: The quality of being uncomfortable, embarrassing, or clumsy.
examples: There was a moment of *awkwardness* before anyone spoke.
He laughed off the *awkwardness* of the introduction.
The *awkwardness* between them lasted for weeks.

gloss: A statement accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point.
examples: Geometry starts from a handful of *axioms*.
It's an *axiom* in this business that the customer decides.
The whole argument rests on one unstated *axiom*.

gloss: A Mexican salamander that keeps its gills and stays in the water all its life.
examples: The pet store had two *axolotls* in a cold tank.
An *axolotl* can regrow a lost limb.
*Axolotls* are critically endangered in the wild.

gloss: The long fiber of a nerve cell that carries signals away from it.
examples: A signal travels down the *axon* to the next cell.
Some *axons* in the spinal cord are more than three feet long.
The diagram labels the cell body, the dendrites, and the *axon*.

gloss: A high-ranking Shia Muslim religious leader.
examples: The *ayatollah* issued a statement on state television.
Several *ayatollahs* opposed the new law.
Reporters waited all day outside the *ayatollah*'s residence.

gloss: A garden shrub that produces masses of bright flowers in spring.
examples: The *azaleas* bloom here in early April.
She planted a row of pink *azaleas* along the fence.
An *azalea* needs acidic soil to do well.

gloss: A bright blue color like a clear sky.
examples: The sky was a deep *azure* by noon.
The painter mixed a pale *azure* for the water.
Nothing beats that Mediterranean *azure*.
contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, AZH-ur, not on the second.

gloss: A headscarf folded into a triangle and tied under the chin.
examples: She tied a *babushka* under her chin before going out.
The old photo shows three women in *babushkas*.
He bought his mother a wool *babushka* at the market.
contrast: In American English *babushka* usually means the headscarf, not the grandmother, and the stress is on the second syllable: buh-BOOSH-kuh.

gloss: A pain in the back, usually a dull lasting one.
examples: I woke up with a bad *backache*.
Lifting boxes all day gave him a *backache*.
Her *backaches* got worse during the pregnancy.

gloss: A movement in which you bend backward until your hands reach the floor.
examples: She can still do a *backbend* at sixty.
The yoga class ended with a gentle *backbend*.
*Backbends* look easier than they actually are.

gloss: The flat board behind a basketball hoop that the ball can bounce off.
examples: The ball bounced off the *backboard* and dropped in.
Someone bent the rim and cracked the *backboard*.
Both *backboards* in the park are made of steel.

gloss: The line of bones down the middle of the back, or the main support of something.
examples: He injured his *backbone* in the fall.
Small farms are the *backbone* of this county.
The X-ray showed a slight curve in her *backbone*.

gloss: A board game for two players using dice and round pieces.
examples: My grandfather taught me *backgammon* one summer.
They play *backgammon* at the café every afternoon.
*Backgammon* is older than chess.

gloss: A stroke in tennis or a similar sport made with the back of the hand facing forward.
examples: Her *backhand* is stronger than her serve.
He returned the shot with a two-handed *backhand*.
Both players have reliable *backhands*.

gloss: A digging machine with a bucket on a jointed arm at the back.
examples: A *backhoe* dug the trench in about an hour.
The city rented two *backhoes* for the water main job.
Watch out — the *backhoe* is backing up.

gloss: Support, especially money or public approval given to a plan or person.
examples: The project has *backing* from two local banks.
She ran for office with the *backing* of the teachers' union.
Without financial *backing*, the film never got made.

gloss: A strong negative reaction from many people to a change or event.
examples: The new policy caused a *backlash* from parents.
There was an immediate *backlash* online.
The company faced a *backlash* over its holiday ad.

gloss: A swimming style in which you lie on your back and move your arms over your head.
examples: She swims *backstroke* better than freestyle.
He won a medal in the 100-meter *backstroke*.
The coach spent all week on our *backstroke*.

gloss: Someone who makes bread, cakes, and pastries.
examples: The *baker* starts work at four in the morning.
Local *bakers* donated bread to the shelter.
She's a talented home *baker*.

gloss: A sweet pastry of thin layers filled with nuts and soaked in honey syrup.
examples: The bakery sells *baklava* by the piece.
She brought a whole tray of homemade *baklava*.
One *baklava* is enough for me — it's very sweet.

gloss: A close-fitting wool hood that covers the head and neck, leaving the face partly open.
examples: The skiers wore *balaclavas* against the wind.
He pulled a black *balaclava* over his face.
A *balaclava* covers everything but your eyes.

gloss: A Russian string instrument with a triangular body and three strings.
examples: He played a few tunes on the *balalaika*.
The group has two *balalaikas* and an accordion.
A *balalaika* is easy to recognize by its triangular shape.

gloss: A game played with a ball, especially a baseball game.
examples: We're taking the kids to a *ballgame* on Saturday.
Rain delayed the *ballgame* by two hours.
Once he joined the team, it was a whole new *ballgame*.

gloss: The study of how bullets and other projectiles travel.
examples: *Ballistics* showed that the shot came from below.
The lab handles fingerprints and *ballistics*.
He studied *ballistics* during his years in the army.
contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb: *Ballistics* is a science.

gloss: Someone who plays baseball or another ball sport, especially professionally.
examples: He was a decent *ballplayer* in high school.
Retired *ballplayers* always show up for the parade.
She's the best *ballplayer* on the block.

gloss: Nonsense, especially something said to fool you.
examples: That excuse is pure *baloney*.
Don't give me any *baloney* about traffic.
He called the whole report *baloney*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *bologna*, the lunch meat; the spelling *baloney* is the one that means nonsense.

gloss: A very light tropical wood used for models and rafts.
examples: The model plane is made of *balsa*.
We cut the wings out of thin *balsa*.
*Balsa* is light enough to float like a cork.

gloss: An official order forbidding something.
examples: The city passed a *ban* on plastic bags.
There's a *ban* on campfires during dry season.
Several *bans* were lifted after the protests.

gloss: A robber, especially one who attacks travelers.
examples: *Bandits* robbed the stagecoach in the old story.
A masked *bandit* held up the bank.
The mountain roads were full of *bandits* back then.

gloss: A small roofed platform in a park where a band plays.
examples: The concert is at the *bandstand* in the park.
Kids were climbing all over the old *bandstand*.
Most town squares around here have a *bandstand*.

gloss: A popular trend that people join because it is succeeding.
examples: Everyone jumped on the *bandwagon* after the team started winning.
Investors climbed aboard the AI *bandwagon*.
He's not a real fan — he's on the *bandwagon*.

gloss: A cause of constant trouble or misery.
examples: Paperwork is the *bane* of every teacher's life.
That squeaky door is the *bane* of my existence.
Mosquitoes were the *bane* of the whole camping trip.

gloss: A sudden loud noise, like something hitting or exploding.
examples: The door shut with a loud *bang*.
We heard a *bang* and then complete silence.
There were two *bangs* from the alley.

gloss: Someone who works at a high level in a bank.
examples: Her father was a *banker* in Chicago.
Investment *bankers* worked through the weekend.
Talk to a *banker* before you sign anything.

gloss: The business of running banks and handling money for customers.
examples: She went into *banking* right after college.
Online *banking* has replaced most branch visits.
The country's *banking* system is heavily regulated.

gloss: The money someone has available to spend or gamble with.
examples: He lost half his *bankroll* on the first night.
The campaign has a serious *bankroll* behind it.
Careful players protect their *bankrolls*.

gloss: A female spirit in Irish folklore whose wailing warns of a death.
examples: The kettle screamed like a *banshee*.
In the story, a *banshee* wails before someone dies.
The twins ran through the house yelling like *banshees*.

gloss: A boxer or fighter in one of the lightest weight classes.
examples: He fought as a *bantamweight* for six years.
The *bantamweight* title is on the line tonight.
Two *bantamweights* opened the card.

gloss: Light, teasing conversation between people who like each other.
examples: There was a lot of friendly *banter* in the locker room.
Their *banter* is what makes the podcast worth hearing.
He mistook the *banter* for a real insult.

gloss: A long metal bar with weights on both ends, lifted with two hands.
examples: She loaded the *barbell* with another twenty pounds.
The gym has six *barbells* and two racks.
Start with an empty *barbell* to learn the movement.

gloss: A powerful drug that calms the nerves or causes sleep.
examples: Doctors rarely prescribe *barbiturates* anymore.
The autopsy found a *barbiturate* in his blood.
*Barbiturates* were replaced by safer sleeping pills.

gloss: A poet who recites or sings stories, especially in older times.
examples: A traveling *bard* sang the story of the battle.
Medieval *bards* memorized hundreds of verses.
In the game she plays a *bard* who fights with music.

gloss: A male singing voice between tenor and bass, or a singer with that voice.
examples: He sings *baritone* in the church choir.
The role was written for a *baritone*.
Two *baritones* auditioned for the part.

gloss: A nobleman of low rank, or a person with great power in an industry.
examples: The land belonged to a local *baron*.
Railroad *barons* built these mansions in the 1890s.
He's known as the cattle *baron* of the valley.
contrast: Sounds the same as *barren* (empty, unable to produce).

gloss: A woman of the rank of baron, or a baron's wife.
examples: The *baroness* opened the charity ball.
Two *baronesses* sit in that chamber.
She married into the family and became a *baroness*.

ru: шквал, град (вопросов и т. п.); артобстрел
gloss: A rapid burst of many things at once, such as gunfire or questions.
examples: The mayor faced a *barrage* of questions.
An artillery *barrage* lasted through the night.
Her inbox got a *barrage* of complaints.

gloss: A neighborhood in a U.S. city where most residents speak Spanish.
examples: He grew up in a *barrio* on the east side.
The murals in the *barrio* draw tourists now.
Several *barrios* organized the food drive together.

gloss: Trade in which goods are exchanged for other goods instead of money.
examples: The village economy still runs partly on *barter*.
Before there was money, *barter* was the only way to trade.
*Barter* works only when each side wants what the other has.

gloss: A hard, dark volcanic rock formed from cooled lava.
examples: The cliffs along this coast are dark *basalt*.
*Basalt* forms when lava cools quickly.
The driveway is covered with crushed *basalt*.

gloss: A large church built as a long hall with side aisles.
examples: We toured a fourth-century *basilica* in the old city.
The *basilica* holds two thousand people.
Several Roman *basilicas* were later turned into churches.

gloss: A musician who plays the bass guitar or double bass.
examples: Their *bassist* writes most of the songs.
The band is looking for a new *bassist*.
Two *bassists* showed up for the audition.
contrast: Said BAY-sist, with the vowel of *base*, not the vowel of the fish *bass*.

gloss: A long wooden wind instrument with a low, deep sound.
examples: She plays *bassoon* in the youth orchestra.
The *bassoon* carries the melody in that passage.
Two *bassoons* sit behind the clarinets.

gloss: A rude word for an unpleasant or unlucky man; historically, a child of unmarried parents.
examples: The poor *bastard* never saw it coming.
He called his old boss a *bastard*.
In the novel, the king's *bastards* fight over the throne.

gloss: A place or group that strongly defends a belief or way of life; also a part of a fort that sticks out.
examples: The college was long a *bastion* of tradition.
The old fort's stone *bastions* still stand.
The union is one of the last *bastions* of that kind of job.

gloss: The reddish rock that aluminum is made from.
examples: Aluminum is refined from *bauxite*.
The country exports *bauxite* to three continents.
*Bauxite* mining has scarred the hillside.

gloss: A blade fixed to the end of a rifle for close fighting.
examples: The soldiers fixed *bayonets* before the charge.
The museum displays a rifle with a rusted *bayonet*.
He was wounded by a *bayonet*, not a bullet.

ru: байу (заболоченный рукав реки на юге США)
gloss: A slow, marshy stream or side channel of a river in the southern United States.
examples: They keep a flat-bottomed boat on the *bayou*.
The *bayous* of Louisiana are full of birds.
Fog sat over the *bayou* all morning.

gloss: A shoulder-fired tube that launches a rocket at tanks or buildings.
examples: The soldier carried a *bazooka* on his shoulder.
*Bazookas* were first used in World War II.
You don't need a *bazooka* to kill a fly.

gloss: A soft bag filled with beads or beans, used as a seat or a toy.
examples: The reading corner has two *beanbags*.
She sank into a huge *beanbag* with her book.
The kids tossed *beanbags* at the target.

gloss: The tall climbing stem of a bean plant.
examples: Jack climbed the *beanstalk* to the giant's castle.
The *beanstalks* need a trellis to climb.
By July the *beanstalk* was taller than the fence.

gloss: A person who carries or presents something.
examples: I hate to be the *bearer* of bad news.
The check is payable to the *bearer*.
Six *bearers* carried the casket to the grave.

gloss: An act of hitting someone repeatedly, or a heavy defeat or loss.
examples: He took a *beating* in the second round.
Our stock took a *beating* this week.
Witnesses described the *beating* in detail.

gloss: A scene of noisy, complete confusion.
examples: It was *bedlam* in the store on Black Friday.
The announcement caused *bedlam* in the hallway.
Three toddlers and one dog equals total *bedlam*.

gloss: A shallow container used as a toilet by someone who cannot get out of bed.
examples: The nurse brought him a *bedpan*.
After surgery he was stuck with *bedpans* and IV lines.
Emptying *bedpans* was her first hospital job.

gloss: One of the four upright posts at the corners of a bed.
examples: He hung his belt on the *bedpost*.
The old bed has four carved *bedposts*.
She banged her knee on the *bedpost* in the dark.

gloss: The solid rock under the soil, or the basic principle something rests on.
examples: They had to drill through *bedrock* to pour the foundation.
Trust is the *bedrock* of any partnership.
The soil here is thin, with *bedrock* just below.

gloss: A skin wound caused by lying in one position for too long.
examples: Nurses turn patients often to prevent *bedsores*.
He developed a *bedsore* after weeks in bed.
*Bedsores* can turn into serious infections.

gloss: A short high electronic sound.
examples: Leave a message after the *beep*.
The microwave gave three *beeps*.
A steady *beep* means the battery is low.

gloss: Someone who lives by asking strangers for money or food.
examples: A *beggar* sat outside the station all winter.
The old city was full of *beggars*.
*Beggars* can't be choosers.

gloss: A common house or garden plant with showy flowers and thick leaves.
examples: She keeps *begonias* on the porch all summer.
A single *begonia* brightened the windowsill.
*Begonias* don't like direct afternoon sun.

ru: имя, интересы (в обороте on behalf of — от имени)
gloss: The interest or support of someone else, used in the phrase on behalf of.
examples: She accepted the award on *behalf* of the whole team.
The lawyer spoke on his client's *behalf*.
On *behalf* of everyone here, thank you.
contrast: Used almost only in *on behalf of* or *on someone's behalf*, never alone.

gloss: The theory that psychology should study observable behavior rather than thoughts.
examples: The course starts with Pavlov and early *behaviorism*.
*Behaviorism* treats the mind as a black box.
Her therapy draws more on *behaviorism* than on Freud.

gloss: A living creature, especially one able to think.
examples: Every human *being* deserves respect.
The film is about *beings* from another planet.
She talks to the dog as if it were a rational *being*.

gloss: A noisy release of gas from the stomach through the mouth.
examples: He let out a loud *belch* and apologized.
The baby's *belch* made everyone laugh.
A few *belches* after soda are perfectly normal.

gloss: The part of a tower where bells hang.
examples: Pigeons nest in the church *belfry*.
The *belfry* is closed to visitors.
Bats hang in both *belfries* on the square.

gloss: A hotel employee who carries guests' luggage and runs errands.
examples: The *bellboy* carried our bags up to the room.
He worked as a *bellboy* one summer in college.
Tip the *bellboy* a couple of dollars.

gloss: The most beautiful and admired woman at an event or in a place.
examples: She was the *belle* of the ball.
The novel's heroine is a Southern *belle*.
Two local *belles* led the parade.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *bell* (the thing that rings).

gloss: A device with folding sides that you squeeze to blow air onto a fire.
examples: He pumped the *bellows* to bring the fire back up.
The blacksmith's *bellows* hung beside the forge.
We keep a small *bellows* by the fireplace.
contrast: Ends in -s in the singular too: *a bellows*, *two bellows*.

gloss: Something that shows how a larger trend is likely to go.
examples: Ohio is often a *bellwether* in national elections.
Housing starts are a *bellwether* for the economy.
Analysts watch a handful of *bellwether* stocks.
contrast: Spelled *-wether* (an old word for a ram), not *weather*.

gloss: The feeling of being accepted as part of a group or place.
examples: The club gave her a real sense of *belonging*.
*Belonging* matters more to teenagers than they admit.
New employees need a feeling of *belonging* early on.
contrast: The plural *belongings* means your possessions, not this feeling.

gloss: A short blessing spoken at the end of a religious service.
examples: The priest gave the *benediction* and the service ended.
A short *benediction* closed the ceremony.
He still remembers the *benedictions* from his childhood church.

gloss: Someone who gives money or help to a person or an institution.
examples: An anonymous *benefactor* paid for the new wing.
The museum thanks its *benefactors* by name each year.
She found a *benefactor* willing to fund the research.

ru: получатель выгоды; наследник по завещанию или страховке
gloss: A person who receives money or an advantage from something.
examples: Name a *beneficiary* on the insurance form.
Small farmers were the main *beneficiaries* of the program.
His sister is the sole *beneficiary* of the will.

gloss: Kindness and a wish to do good for others.
examples: The hospital depends on the *benevolence* of donors.
He ruled with a mix of *benevolence* and fear.
Her *benevolence* toward strangers was well known.

gloss: A clear, sweet-smelling liquid chemical used in industry and known to cause cancer.
examples: *Benzene* in the groundwater forced the town to close its wells.
The lab only handles *benzene* under a fume hood.
Gasoline contains small amounts of *benzene*.
contrast: False friend: *benzene* is the chemical бензол; Russian «бензин» is *gasoline* in American English.

gloss: Money or property left to someone in a will.
examples: The library was built with a *bequest* from a former teacher.
She left small *bequests* to each of her nieces.
The museum received a generous *bequest* last spring.
